utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic also know as Vlado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. No translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to inform the Tribunal that Prosecution is today represented also by Mr. Bill Smith, who is behind me, and who will express himself in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We go on with Counsel Radovic. I think Counsel Radovic would like to continue cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness N. Good morning. May we continue? You said that you worked in a former institution department of the JNA for repair work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the former JNA when I did my military service. I was in charge of weapons, maintenance of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And did you come across the Browning type of machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I encountered this weapon the first time during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know a Browning is made in Sweden, is a Swedish product then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I encountered a case of that kind, that is a weapon of that kind, taken over by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was that Browning like? What was it like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Describe it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to describe. There is a stand, a support, which is separate, and on one of the supports levers. You have the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many supports has that particular weapon got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw it the first time, it had three legs, a tripod type.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And the upper half?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's more or less correct, except that it is not Swedish made but made in the USA That's the difference. You said yesterday that an individual gave you some money to make a statement, and that you refused this. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. There were several, and it's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's important to me, so I would like to hear what you remembered about that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But if they offered you money, they told you what they were offering you money for, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they probably wanted to learn something they were interested in knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you must have told somebody something they needed to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not -- for their own fame, but it didn't mean anything for me. Well, for people of that kind, journalists and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how come that it was only in May 1998 that you appeared, let me say, in front of the Bosnian intelligence service, secret service? How did they reach you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I made no statements to them because they took statements -- the statement from one of my colleagues, and then just crossed it out and wrote the same thing and wrote just my name and so on, the same thing that he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that colleague's statement? Did you sign anything on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me yesterday. Yes, I remember now. It was on one particular day. He asked me whether I agreed with what he had stated. And me and my colleague, we were pals, we were together when all this happened. He was with me on the night -- that particular night. He came home from work. He worked in Vitez at Vidovic's place, the baker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the colleague who came to testify with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he refused to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He works a lot, he has a lot of responsibilities, and he said that he won't be able to make up for lost time financially, and, therefore, he did not agree to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us what this was like? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you started saying something about how you and your colleague went together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. He worked in the bakery, Vidovic's bakery, in Vitez. I forget the name. And he came late for work, and he said that he would spend the night in my house because there was something going on on the road, that there was a lot of army and that they were combat equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And he told you this, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where did he tell you this? The Gamija (phoen) area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, where I lived. Where I was living. He came to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested in knowing about the part when you said you went to the police, the A-I-D, AID police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know what they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. But you went there and what did that look like? Because you said that you talked to him, whereas they kept asking you whether you agreed with what he had said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to repeat everything -- they didn't want to repeat everything, so they just sort of photocopied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And then you signed this photocopied statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you sign it if it was not your statement? Because it states that, the citizen has read and sign the statement, he has no comments to make on it and is ready to testify to all this before a court. Why did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to prevent me repeating the whole story once again, because it was the same story. That was why.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So, in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to prevent -- so -- because his statement lasted the whole day. The talks lasted the whole day. It was very boring, and it's very boring to keep repeating the same thing over and over again. There are a lot of people who want to know what happened, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who was bored? You were bored to have to repeat the story over and over again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, let me tell you. Let me explain. For me, I -- everybody is interested in knowing what happened. Everybody asked me what happened, those are in charge and have a responsibility and others, and so I have to keep repeating this. I experienced a great deal of terrible things. I have traumas, so I don't wish to go into all the whole matter again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have one more question that I was not quite clear on to ask you. You said there was shooting from a sniper on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it was shooting from a sniper and not a gun without a sight, without optic sights? How do you know that it was a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was on the spot where two men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's all right. But do you think you can't kill somebody with an M-40 rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that distance, no, quite definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us hear the distance between the person doing the shooting and the victim of the shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Come on. We've all done our military service. Let's see what we remembered from those days and that training.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was below the road. About 200 metres, would I say, a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the range with the M-48 rifle without an optic sight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would have to be a very good marksman, a excellent marksman to kill someone at that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. Never mind. I've concluded my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Tell me, please, who came to Ahmici with you when you arrived there in August 1992, apart from your family. Who else was there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had my sister-in-law -- three sisters-in-law, and their husbands had died in Prijedor before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about your family, I want to know about the other people who remained in Ahmici with you later on. First of all, the man that you mentioned having signed an identical statement, was it Rifet Hustic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you testified together you were at the secret police together and you gave one statement. That is to say you gave the same identical statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In fact, you signed his statement, that is what it was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when it was photocopied. I signed my paper, he signed his.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And did he go to Ahmici with you on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did he -- did Serif Omanovic come with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, did he.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was Rahim Music there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And was Muradif Cikotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they come with their families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cikotic had nobody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other one did have his family with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me whether their families, wives and children had gone to Austria like your own family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rahim Music, yes. They had nowhere to go, Rahim Music, because they were waiting to get papers. They didn't have anybody to get them their papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about Huskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He got papers for his wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about Cikotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he had nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about Omanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And did she go to Austria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had lived in Austria. She had been living in Austria for a long time, and she was a citizen of Austria. She'd been a citizen for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether you know that at that time there was a state of general mobilisation for Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was voluntary. Later on, when the war began in full swing, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But at that time, it was October 1992, at that time were conscripts banned from leaving Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you not have to have some special papers to be able to leave Bosnia if you were a conscript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You needed documents from the HVO and from the army, and it was difficult to get them anyway, even if you did request that these papers be issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So it was difficult. These papers were not readily at hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When you got the papers, this was still not guarantee and you had no Visa to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you stayed there and the wives and children would go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you employed at that time anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Before the war I was an engine driver at the railways, and there was nowhere for me to work because there were no railways, so there was no work. No trains, no work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that, in fact, you guarded people saying prayers in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was sort of watch duty, guard duty that we had decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This was during the day, in the early morning at dawn and towards evening when prayers were said in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we had previous experience which showed us that accidents and these unfortunate occurrences happened -- occurred when -- during prayer time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes. So, in fact, you were on guard duty during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you not have any night duty like the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether you were exclusively in charge of guarding the mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only me, but we would take it in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You couldn't have one man doing guard duty all the time so there were more individuals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had our schedule for guarding the mosque during the day and during prayer time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you, in fact, hired by Hazim Ahmic, the hadja? Did you do this in co-operation with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was not in good relations -- did not have good relations with him because he was very gullible. He was illiterate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the people who guarded the mosque, where did they sleep? Did any of them sleep in the school building or in the mosque itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those people slept at home, in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that means that they did not sleep in the school building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me how many people were in charge of guarding the mosque. The others would -- how many people in all, do you know, approximately, the people that rotated in doing guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one man a day during the day. That was enough, because there were people around and the houses were in close proximity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When people would go to do their guard duty, would they take weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't. No weapons in the mosque as some people would have us believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I don't mean that they were in the mosque. I suppose that they were on guard duty outside the mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you asked whether they took weapons into the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, no. I meant those doing guard duty outside the mosque, and did they carry weapons for that guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had weapons. That was quite normal, because there was the imminent danger of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Where did they keep those weapons, at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they kept them at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At home, you say. What kind of weapons did they have usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they usually had old rifles, not very potent rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were in charge of guard duty to protect the mosque with that kind of rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the number, but from this particular place I know the people who were involved in the war, and at that time they all fought at Visoko against the Chetniks. You know where Visoko is, it's near Sarajevo at Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right and what happened with those rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the better weaponry they took with them, because on the front-line you couldn't repair weapons. You had no time to repair your weapons. You go there and there was a lot of dying. So all the older rifles remained in the village. There were women and children in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people were there in Ahmici, in your assessment? Could there have been 1.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as many, no. Certainly not as many.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, tell us then. You give us an estimate. Six hundred would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's see. In every house there would be one old man usually per household in every house, and perhaps two other people who were able to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, does that -- shall we say 200?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two hundred, yes. Unfortunately, those who were at Zume had surrendered their arms and they were told that they would be safe, but unfortunately, they were all killed and that's something that should be taken note of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the arms surrendered anywhere else apart from Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Ahmici, but I don't know how many weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You don't know how many. Tell us, did the villagers -- were they members of the 323rd Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were members, and they had to go to the battlefield, to Visoko. Mostly they were sent to Visoko, practically always.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And did they maintain the positions towards the Serbs at Vlacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in Visoko this is the line towards the Serbs. At Valasici the positions were held by those from Turbe, Travnik, Bugojno and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the people from the villages -- were they on the battlefield in Busovaca in January and February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they went to fight there because it was too far off. Well, not actually far off, but that was what the schedule, the distribution was. Some of the officers would give these orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How far is Busovaca from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you would have to go to Zenica, and then from Zenica to the battlefield. And people in Zenica were mobilised, so there was no need for them to go to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that means that they would go to Visoko which was further off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a problem there because the locals, for example, the local people were not -- there were problems with the locals there. They refused to go to the -- to war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about 1993, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they thought that the Chetniks would not attack them there because they were good people, and when you were lulled in this way you would get what was coming to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, that was later on. I'm asking you about the period that I mentioned, the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was like that at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That means that there were problems at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when there's war there are always problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, you said that you -- when you were informed by Rifet Huskic that he had seen some armed soldiers wearing helmets on the road home, that after that you had informed the command of the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rifet told me but I did not inform anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I think that I was too tired, and I went to sleep very early, so I was able to get up early.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you inform Hazim Ahmic perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had no discussion was him. His wife was a very fine woman, but he was not a fine man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, tell me where Rifet Huskic slept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He slept in the cottages down below, Milecivic and so on, below the road, below the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did he sleep in Vehbija Ahmic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He slept for a time, he stayed for a time and then moved to the weekend cottage because Vehbija had a large family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did he sleep on that particular night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He slept in my house on that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did he sleep in that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came from work late.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you agree to have more of you in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a sort of preventative measure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That means that you and he knew that something was boiling, and did you not inform anybody about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was to have gone down below the road, where Hrustanovic with his family was, but he informed them, and they all came to my place and we all spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That means they were all in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether the command, the TO command in the village, was informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the command, "The TO command in the village, although it had been informed of this, did not believe there would be an attack" because they had allegedly reached an agreement with the HVO. You also said that you know that the Hadzija from Ahmici negotiated with you -- they had promised not to attack the village, and they elected Hadzija for the negotiator because the people believed the Hadzija, which means from this that you, in fact, did talk to the commander of the TO, that you informed him, you informed the Hadzija, and you now state that none of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not inform them. Perhaps Huskic did, but on that particular night, I went to sleep very early, as I said, so I don't know what happened in the course of the night. I was on duty during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: As a preventive measure, you were all together in the house, you were informed of the possible problems on that particular night, and you say that you went to sleep early and slept throughout the night without any problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not everybody slept. You didn't understand me. I did guard duty during the day, and so I had to sleep at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, who was on duty at night there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was asleep. How can I know if I was asleep?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what was the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No agreement. I don't know about any agreement. How could I know about an agreement when I was sleeping?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you with Hazrudin Bilic the night before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that the radio station was in the school building close to the mosque? You could know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was where a relation of mine, Husic Music, and his family lived. I went there frequently. There was no radio station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And Husic Rahim was also a refugee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the TO command meet in the school building ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did they meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in the village, but I did not attend the meetings, any meetings of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you became included into the TO in Ahmici. There must have been a meeting, or was this Huskic's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was a guest, but as you know, I'm from another part, a foreigner, so to speak, so it was not usual for foreigners to be told anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know by sight, people by sight, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were involved with the TO, approximately? Was it one company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all those who thought that they could do guard duty did guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me whether you had ever been to Preocica for a review of some kind, a military review of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you take an oath of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, at the beginning, it was either the TO or the Patriotic League, as we used to call it. At the beginning. There were no oaths to be taken there. The Patriotic League was your patriotic duty, to help the people as much as you could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after that, I was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina till the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Since what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they drew me in so that I could have those --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did they engage you, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici, they would have some problems with the old rifles, and so usually people would use the rifles and shoot but they did not clean them, and so they did not know how to deal with this. The biggest problem was because the rifles were not cleaned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes. I would take their rifles and clean them and see to the maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, when did you take the oath and when did you become a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no oaths. I took no oath. It is only the young recruits which take the oath; that is, when you were a soldier, recruit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, since when do you consider yourself to be a soldier of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. In my military book, military record, I have 43 months listed and ninety -- I was demobilised in 1996, in August, so you can count back and calculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, that is. Well, it's not up to me to do the counting and calculations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Forty-six months backwards, then. Did you get any supplies from the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, food and lodging.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992 and 1993, any rations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cigarettes, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about food, lodging you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, later on, when the war was in full swing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you live on if you didn't have any resources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I was given lodgings, which was usually in the village, I slept in a house in the village, and with the person you lived with, you would have your -- take your meals there, where you were billeted, but, of course, they knew that I was a refugee and had nothing of my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that went by the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was the duty of the villagers, of the locals, to feed somebody that they would take in, the lodgers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So how many people in the village were billeted whose families had left and who had become members of the BH army and who were sent to a lodge with the villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there weren't many people like that, and my family was to have returned because they did not -- they were not happy where they went, but I told them not to come because the situation was very difficult and that they should have a little more patience.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many refugees were there in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, about the 16th, when was the mosque in the village shot down? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see it personally. We were withdrawing with the civilians towards Zenica. This was -- I think it was in the forest above the village, between Vrhovine and Ahmici, and a very strong detonation was heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was that in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Exactly at 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the same day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- well, whether it was 10.00 p.m. or 11.00 p.m., but anyway, there was a strong detonation, a strong explosion. We didn't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, when did you arrive in Upper Ahmici? What was the time; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we arrived at about 2.00 p.m., thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you withdraw upwards towards Vrhovine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not able to go further because there is no forest above the village. About half a kilometre. So had we gone up there, we would have been shot at. So we had to wait for dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there some shooting on that afternoon and evening when you withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was shooting, but not very strong. The intensity was less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Less intensity, yes. Tell me, on the 17th of April, the line was formed above the village, above Pirici and Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the dates. It is not a later date; it was the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the defence line set up? Where was the army stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Zenica afterwards and they engaged me again and I had -- there was -- everybody was given their duties and responsibilities. Somebody had to see to the rifles, others had to see to the food and supplies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know that the line, defence line, was formed above Ahmici which remained throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not remain there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The line was set up and there was a field between Barica Gaj and the upper part of the village and it was a clear space, and later on the HVO, after I don't know exactly how much time elapsed, but they launched an attack and took control of part of Barica Gaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that later on. Could you just please tell me whether, with other people from the village, you set up the line? Were you up there with them at Barica Gaj on the second day when you had come from Vrhovine? We're talking about the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Not later on. I'm asking about the 17th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a very strong line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, not a strong line, but did the HVO try to move forward, and that was the line at which you stopped the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a demarcation line and sporadic gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many villagers were up at the line from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Two, five, or twenty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From which village?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Ahmici. And I'm thinking about the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. I wasn't there in fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, were there two or twenty? Can you give us a rough estimate, or were there fifty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were about twenty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: About twenty, you say. Did any help arrive from Zenica, any units from Zenica, reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, each unit had its part of the territory for which it was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which means then that that part of the line was guarded by the people from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahmici, Vrhovine, Prnjavor and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pretenica and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You can't actually say -- I don't know what you meant by saying -- it would appear that they were all mobilised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not all mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were all mobilised. I just asked how many people from Ahmici were up at the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not everybody could have been there. If you know anything about war and the conditions governing war, you can't have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can't have everybody mobilised because some people are ill, others are incapable, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. I understand. But let me say once again that your statement is quite different. I don't know if this is your statement or Huskic Rifet's statement, but it states that immediately in the morning on the 17th of April, 1993, the HVO soldiers tried to move forward, but that you were assisted by a unit from Zenica and that you succeeded in setting up a defence line and repelling the attacks, and the line remained where it was until the peace agreement was negotiated with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me about details.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But that is your statement, that is to say, the statement of your friend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it finished very quickly -- you know, if you're interrogated for a whole day, interviewed for a whole day, can you imagine me answering questions all day by a gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you answer any questions on that particular occasion or was it just Huskic Rifet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was him. He answered most of the questions. He thought he would go and testify, and later on, it turned out that he was frightened. He's not very literate either, and so he gave up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. I wonder whether the Prosecutor would like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (In French) Mr. Terrier, there was no translation in English. No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a problem with one of the pieces of equipment in the booth. You can carry on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Maybe I could proceed in English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please continue in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Usher -- yes, I was just saying that I wished to clarify this issue of the statement, whether there is some confusion. For the time being, Mr. Usher, could you submit this document to Witness N? It is a document drafted in Bosniak, it is a three-page long document with the name of the witness and the date of the 6th of May, 1992. As I initially said to the Tribunal, there is a misprint there. It is the 6th of May, 1998 and not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness N, is this your statement, and can you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it is your signature indeed. Is it your statement, the statement you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. It is something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please, would you mind submitting the second document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked 184 and the earlier document 183.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It is a four-page document in the Bosnian language, a statement made by Rifet Huskic. Would you be in a position to compare these two documents and confirm that these are two very different documents, different one from the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They cannot be different because we were there together when the events took place. There is something which perhaps is not all that identical. He wrote about the details, how he worked in Vitez, where he worked, this and that. He went into all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness N, when I state that these documents are different, of course, we're not talking about different facts you are witnessing, you're testifying about facts that you experienced together. These are the very same facts. But I'm saying that one document is not a copy of the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Factually, it turns out that in order not to have to ask me all the same things all over again, this has been copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Witness N, you may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, I assume we are all moving to the old No. 2. I'm afraid we don't know what protective measures you have envisaged for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This witness has requested face and name protection, and I will also inform the Court at this time that he does not read, and so the oath will, I think, have to be dictated to him orally because he cannot read the oath. He does, however -- can recognise his name in writing, so that can be done without a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It will be Witness O?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness O. I would like to ask you to repeat the solemn declaration which will be read out by our registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat after me? "I solemnly declare ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "... that I will speak the truth ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... that I will speak the truth ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "... the whole truth ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... the whole truth ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "... and nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, I will hand to the usher a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness O.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You might want to pull your chair up a little bit so you can speak directly into the microphone. Thank you. You have requested --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You have requested certain measures for your protection, and I want to inform you that they have been granted, so you can feel comfortable in providing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- your evidence here today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: To begin with, Witness O, could you tell us in what year you were born?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your home village was before 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have to leave Karaula in about 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, I had -- we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left Karaula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: We went to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall in which house you lived in in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: The house of one Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would this be Ramiz Gradinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did you know about the house of Ramiz Gradinovic and know that you could live there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: We came searching from up there when we were expelled from Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you in any way related to Ramiz Gradinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall about what month you and your family arrived in Ahmici and began to live in the house of Ramiz Gradinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: It was in November in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Without naming any particular individual in your family, could you just tell us the composition of your family at that time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: How do you mean? To tell you how many members of my family there were?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exactly, and whether you had any children, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, there were five children with me and my wife. Three sons and two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember the day of the attack in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: On the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I want you to, before we discuss that day, focus your attention on the day before the attack, April 15, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: The 15th. Yes. It was a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what you were doing on that day, the day before the attack, April 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I went to Zume to one Marko Vrebac because my horse and cart were there, I wanted him to repair my cart, and he told me that there was not enough electric power so that he couldn't repair it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall where you went after checking on your cart in Zume?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Then I went to Pican's cafe with Jure Vrebac for a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a drink with that individual at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, we had a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you go after that, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: We went up there to the playing ground, to the -- the road towards Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was this on your way to go back home to the house of Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: That's where I was going. I took the road to home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see anything around that area as you were walking home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I saw a vehicle, a large lorry, and there was something on it, probably an anti-aircraft gun or a canon. It was covered by tarpaulin, so I couldn't tell. It was protected, covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What made you think it was probably an anti-aircraft gun or some sort of weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: 'Cause I've seen things like that around, and there I then again saw that kind of a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you then continue on to the house you were living in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, I went walking towards home and I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, sometime that evening, did you have an opportunity to be outside the home of Ramiz where you saw something interesting or unusual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes. I saw some troops near Ramiz's house and also down in front of Vlatko's house. Actually, four or five or six soldiers I saw. I don't know exactly. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You say it was dark. How could you see these troops if it was dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Well, it was around 6.00. It was dusk, rather, so I could tell that there were that many people or thereabouts there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you say "there," where were these troops that you saw that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: By Vlatko's house, actually, in Vlatko's house's yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask the usher show to the witness previously admitted Exhibit 32, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Witness O, could you take a look at this exhibit that we've called Exhibit 32 and tell us if you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What is this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: That is Vlatko's house. Near the greenery here in the corner is the spot where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you help us a little bit by taking that pointer you have next to your hand, yes, thank you, and could you point to the picture not on the TV screen but on the picture next to you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: This is where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- with the help of the usher, and tell us where you saw the soldiers that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: This is where the soldiers were, here on this spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a pretty good view, from where you were standing, of that spot that you just pointed to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a good view. I was standing up there by Ramiz's house, near the water fountain, right there, and I could see them well. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you tell anybody what you had seen, that you had seen several soldiers in front of Vlatko's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, I told nobody. I didn't make much of it. I didn't think it was that important. I told nobody about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you know a person by the name of Marinko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I have seen him on occasion in front of Vlatko's store. Their name is Sutra. And he told me he would be leaving these parts very quickly. Once as I was hauling some wood I stopped by there and I had a beer there, and he told me, "You will be leaving these parts very soon, on the 1st of May. " And I thought that we would be going to Karaula, to our house, but it was not to Karaula, they attacked us before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You said he told you that you would be leaving these parts very soon. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He did say that. Marinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And where did he tell you this? Where were you when he told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: In front of Sutra's store, or his storehouse, and it is called "Sutra", something like that, just above Vlatko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And do you recall about when that conversation took place, maybe how many days before the attack, if you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some seven or eight or even ten days prior to the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And when Marinko told you this, what did you think he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I thought that he really knew that we were going back, that we would be going back to Karaula, to our own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, in retrospect, or looking back on it, what do you think he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I don't know what he was talking about, what he had in mind, whether he wanted us to go back to our place or something else, or to expel us from that area, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Then just to be clear, do you know whether Marinko was a Croat who lived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, going back to the evening before the attack, April 15, do you recall what you did that night after -- or before the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I was doing guard duty with Ramiz, in the patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What about Ramiz, did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Ramiz had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "guard duty"? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Well, we guarded the village. Sort of patrolled it to see that there wasn't any shooting or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was this patrol, this village guard, was this like an army? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Well, it was a sort of village watch, a village patrol, not an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what you recall about the next morning, April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I remember I got up in the morning, I was at Zume, and somebody told me I was to go plough a garden. So I got up that morning. It was quarter to four. It was quarter to four in the morning, and I went out to the toilet, and there was a slight drizzle. I went back into the house and didn't go anywhere. Then I got up again because my daughter was to go to work, and I got up again. It was about 5.00, 5.00 a.m. And I went outside, I lit a cigarette, and went to the barn, and there was some enormous -- this was about 5.30. I couldn't even get to the barn, didn't -- and shooting started. I just went back and I said to my children, "Get up, because we'll all be shot." And I rushed up to my wife, who was in the weekend cottage, to see whether my wife and daughter had got up. And I went in front of Redzib's house. A mortar fell and it hit me here on the left -- my left shoulder. And when I got my left shoulder, there was no blood but something had hit me. And as I was once wounded, I was frightened, and I thought here it comes again, I'm wounded again, and that was where I was. When I rushed up, my wife, she was wearing her underwear, apologise, but she was wearing her underwear, and she said that they fired across the windows. And my daughter said, "Take my son, my child, for me, to get my trousers on, pants on." She took her pants and I gave her back the child, and I went back to see what was happening in front. I looked through the window to see what was happening in front of the weekend cottage, and there were six soldiers with weapons going towards the house, and they were carrying weapons. And they went down to Huso's house. They killed Huso, they killed him straight away, and Sukrija, and the like. They killed them all, anybody they came across. And Huso's wife said, "They killed Huso in front of my very eyes. Let's flee with the children." And I was terribly frightened, because I am -- look like an able-bodied man. They don't know, in fact, that I am somebody who was wounded. So I said to my wife, "Let's get out of here." And my mother said, "Well, we" -- my wife said, "We lost everything in Karsula. Let them kill us all, and we can lose -- we've got nothing to lose everything here." "But God help you I'm going to escape because they're going to kill me." And I fled about a hundred metres away, and I went back for them and I told them again, "Come on, let's go, because what is going to happen to our -- our daughters, what will happen to us? Let's all go together." So we went up to Vrhovine and we stayed there a little while. There was shooting down below. I went back once again because I had left some money down there. So I went back for my money, but I wasn't able to even approach the village because there was a lot of crying and shooting down below. I don't know what was happening, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let me just ask a couple of questions before you go on, Witness O, to clarify some things. You said that early in the morning you remember going to the bathroom. Is this an inside bathroom or did you have to go outside in order to use the facility, the toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, apologise. I had to go out. It was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And when you went outside --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: And I saw the lights on that morning in Vlatko house. It was 15 -- or 4.00 in the morning, but I didn't know that they would be attacking, and it was really a great misfortune, and I didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated that a mortar fell and you suffered some sort -- or you felt something. Where were you when that mortar fell, or that shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Near -- by Redzib's house. And the mortar shell hit Redzib's house and I was there next to it. And something hit me in my left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you also said, I believe, that you were wounded. Just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I was wounded. I was wounded and I was wounded before in 1992, up there in Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you wounded that day in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: As you fled Ahmici, did you look back at the village at any point and could you see what was happening to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I did see that the village -- as we were fleeing, I did see that the village was ablaze. There was all sorts of shouting and crying by the people that could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you now recall in particular any houses that you can identify that you saw on fire as you left Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Suad's house was on fire, Redzib's house was also on fire. He actually went back to put the fire out, and as he returned he was killed on the spot. Ramiz's house was also on fire. As we reached that point up there, we could see that everything was burning down there. Suad's and Redzib's house were set on fire immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you and your family manage to flee Ahmici without anyone being -- any one of your family members being injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, we managed to flee to Vrhovine. No one was hurt -- no one was injured in my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I just have one moment, Mr. President? We have no more questions for this witness, and we request that the exhibits, piece of paper, I don't know the number right now, be admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: 185, thank you. Be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can inform you that colleague Radovic will have a few questions to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I really have only a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I am the Defence counsel of one of the accused, Radovic. The first request is: How could you know that there was an anti-aircraft machine gun or cannon when it was covered by tarpaulin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I could see there was some kind of weapon. It had to be an anti-aircraft gun or a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could it have been a machine, a similarly shaped machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have been a machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But how can you conclude that it had to be precisely an anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Because I saw this passing from -- to Busovaca and Vitez, this truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. How did you know that what was covered by the tarpaulin was a cannon, a PAT?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I didn't say PAT, I said cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But a PAT is a cannon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I said there was something and it had to be a PAM or a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But how did you know that either of these two things was under the tarpaulin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Because I've seen things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But was the tarpaulin ever removed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, but you could see it was stretched around the shape of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But there could have been logs under it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, there couldn't have been logs under it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot demonstrate this to you because I do not have the technical means for that, but okay, never mind, let's move on. Of course, everyone is entitled to their opinion. Tell me about the visibility at 5.30 in the morning when the shooting started on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: It was good. It was good. The visibility was good. There was some rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any fog?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, there was some fog but not too much of it. It was just slightly misty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, at 5.30, when you came in front of the house, what was the weather like? You said there was rain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, there was a slight rain. There was a slight drizzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that the lights were on in the houses, the electric power lights, or was it possible to see the houses on the basis of daylight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: But at 4.15 there were lights at Vlatko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At 5.30 when everything started -- when the shooting started, you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were there lights then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No. I had no time to look. I was so terrified I had to flee. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You said you were on guard duty with Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: But it was not station duty but patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So when you were on guard duty or patrolling around, when you noticed something suspicious, what was your obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: We had to inform the people in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "the people in the village"? You had to inform a specific person or the whole village? Who was in charge of being informed of such occurrences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: We were told to alarm the village, to inform the people that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But how could you inform the entire village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Well, I would come to your house and say, "We have noticed some troops," or this and that, "We have been attacked, let's flee."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you would go from house to house and orally inform the people. But you did not have a sort of a signal, or a siren, or a firing of a round to inform the people, you went from house to house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, we had nothing of that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much time it would take you to inform everyone house by house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: But it goes as a chain, because I would inform one house, and then they would inform the next household, and it would be sort of relayed from house to house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: There was something that was not quite clear, in your statement, to me. You said that the Croats attacked you before the order, literally. You said before the schedule, before the order what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: We didn't know they would attack us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But what does that mean, that phrase, "before their schedule"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: But I would have fled had I known that they would attack, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So when you said, "They attacked us before their turn or before the schedule," what you meant is that you were taken by surprise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Had I known, I would have fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just want to know what you meant when you said, "They attacked us ahead of schedule," but now you have explained that what you meant is actually that you were -- they launched a surprise attack so that you couldn't flee. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I only have one question. You mentioned some soldiers who were coming towards the direction of this weekend cottage, you saw six soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: From which direction were they coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: From up there they came, and they surrounded the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where is this "up there"? What houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Above Krdzo's house, from where the road leads to the Sutra's house and to Zume. From there they came. They killed two people on guard duty in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see those six soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did they look?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: They had motley suits, uniforms. And they went towards Krdzo's house, and Krdzo's wife rushed up --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did you look at it from -- Krdzo's house is this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: They were advancing like that down towards the garden. I saw it with my very eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And they went into Krdzo's house. What did they do? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: His wife said that they killed him. They shot him right there immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then where did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: How should I know where they went from there?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you just said that they went on towards -- you said that after they killed Huso, they went to Sutra -- Sukrija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, they killed Sukrija, Naser, his brother. They killed them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they -- did you see them going down towards Sukrija's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. I certainly did. That was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was at the beginning? First of all, you heard this shell.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: First there was firing. There was infantry fire, then a shell fell, then a shell land at the house, when I was near the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then you saw these soldiers at the very beginning, and you saw them going towards --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, Huso's and Krdzo's house, down through the garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they enter the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot say. His wife came and said, "They have killed Huso and they killed him before my very eyes."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then they went down towards Sukrija's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, they did, toward Sukrija's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see the insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No. 17 Q. Did they have any caps? 18 A. They had some sort of winter cap on which didn't show their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they have any helmets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't notice any helmets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, I saw weapons. They had rifles, they had automatic weapons. And I didn't notice anything else. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: No, no, because I hadn't lived there. I didn't know the people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you saw that they were going down towards Sukrija's house, did you see that they were also going into the house of Meho Hrustanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: I saw them going from Huso's house to Meho's house. Meho was killed immediately. So they were going from Huso's house, to Meho Hrustanovic's house and then to Sukrija's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, because I know I had my horses there in Meho Hrustanovic's barn, and, actually, I wasn't able to go there that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that was at the very beginning of the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that moment, what was the first house to be set on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: It was, I believe, Suad's house that was first torched. Ahmic, yes. I'm not sure. And then a shell also landed in the house of his father, Redzib, and something fell on my arm, on my shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any houses in your part of the village, the lower part of the village, burn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: That was where the first house was set on fire that I saw. Redzib went to extinguish the fire on his house but he never returned. He was killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was Redzib before he returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: He was -- he was up there where a concrete slab was above his house. Somebody had started constructing a house and there he was. And when he saw that his house was ablaze, he returned down to put the fire out and he never came back. He was killed right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you told my colleague that there was a slight rain, a drizzle and mist. Was it visible at half past five?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was good. Of course it was. It was the 16th of April, you could see well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It was daylight, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz, would you like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Witness O, thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, I suggest we now take a break, and I wonder whether you could bring in the next witness, if it is number 5, so that when we reconvene we already have the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Bill Smith and I appear for the Prosecutors in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skillen. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
